summary.title: The return of fancy tools
summary.one_liner: Tom MacWright argues that tools swing between complexity and simplicity, and that friction in simple tools, like hand-typed note names and fuzzy file search, can build memory that frictionless fancy tools do not.
keywords: why simple tools make you think
takeaways: Tools cycle between complexity and simplicity; newer tools often fix the previous tool's problems while adding new ones.
Structured editors like Notion tend to encourage overstructuring, where the schema does not match how people actually think about information.
Easy-to-add features, such as scroll-fade effects in Webflow, get used simply because the button exists.
Friction in plain-text note-taking and manual linking is argued to produce memory, not just notes.
The author keeps editor navigation simple (neovim with fzf) so that names and how code fits together live in the mind.
summary.summary: This short essay by Tom MacWright on his blog traces a pattern of technology swinging between complexity and simplicity, citing examples such as Dreamweaver, Webflow, Evernote, Notion, Visual Studio, VS Code, JIRA, GitHub issues and Linear. He criticises overstructured editors and easy-to-add effects, then defends a deliberate amount of friction in note-taking and code navigation. He ties this to a Drucker quote about writing things down to remember them now. It is an opinion piece with no code or step-by-step instructions.
